title: Genesis 7. The Cup Poured Out.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 7. The Cup Poured Out.
The Lord says to Noah: Come into the ark,
you and all your household.
For I have seen that you are righteous before Me in this generation.
The word is not "go.
The word is "come.
God is already inside.
He invites Noah into a space He occupies first.
The Cup that was designed in chapter six now receives the man it was built for.
Seven pairs of clean animals.
Two of every unclean animal.
Seven pairs of birds,
to keep seed alive on the face of all the earth.
The creatures come to Noah.
He does not chase them.
He does not hunt them.
He does not herd them.
They come.
The same God who said "let the waters teem" in chapter one now speaks to every living thing and says:
go to the man.
The Cup is being filled, and the creatures come on their own.
In seven days, the rain will fall.
Forty days and forty nights.
Every living thing I have made,
I will blot out from the face of the ground.
Noah does everything the Lord commands him.
He is six hundred years old.
The floodwaters come.
Noah enters the ark with his sons,
his wife and his sons' wives.
The animals come, clean and unclean, birds, creeping things, two by two,
male and female.
They enter as God commanded.
Then the Lord shuts him in.
Noah did not close the door.
God closed the door.
The same God who opened the boundary between light and darkness,
between water above and water below,
now closes the boundary between the saved and the drowned.
The door is in the side of the ark,
and the hand that shut it is the same hand that once walked in the garden in the cool of the day and called:
Where are you?
On the seventeenth day of the second month,
in the six hundredth year of Noah's life, on that day,
all the fountains of the great deep burst open,
and the windows of the heavens were opened.
What God separated in chapter one, He now unites.
On day two, He divided the waters, water above from water below,
and called the expanse sky.
Now the waters below erupt from the deep.
The waters above pour through the windows of heaven.
The boundary that held creation together comes undone.
The structure that was spoken into formlessness returns toward formlessness.
The rain falls for forty days and forty nights.
The waters increase.
The ark is lifted up above the earth.
The waters rise and increase greatly.
The ark floats on the surface of the waters.
The vessel that God designed,
built by a man who walked with Him, sealed with pitch,
filled with every kind of creature, holds.
The smaller Cup rises above the larger one.
Inside the judgment, life persists.
The waters rise higher.
Every high mountain under the whole sky is covered.
Fifteen cubits above the highest peaks.
The peaks that were raised on day three,
when dry land appeared and was called earth, they are gone.
The land that received Abel's blood, that was cursed for Cain,
that was worked by sweat and thorns, is buried.
What was formed is unformed.
What was filled is flooded.
All flesh that moves on the earth dies.
Birds.
Livestock.
Animals.
Every creeping thing.
Every man.
All in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life,
everything on dry land, died.
The breath that God breathed into man in chapter two returns to the waters.
The animals that were brought to Adam to be named are gone.
The birds that flew on day five,
the creatures that teemed in the sea,
the livestock that was given for food, gone.
Every living thing on the face of the ground was blotted out.
Man, livestock, creeping things, birds of the sky.
They were blotted out from the earth.
Only Noah remained, and those who were with him in the ark.
The Cup that was filled at creation has been poured out.
What was spoken into existence has been spoken back into the deep.
The grief God felt in chapter six has been answered,
not with more words, but with water.
The earth that God saw and called good is now water as far as the eye can see.
And the waters prevailed on the earth for a hundred and fifty days.
No one inside the ark knows when the water will stop.
No one knows what the world will look like when it recedes.
The door is shut.
The rain has stopped, but the water remains.
What began with warning has become a silence while the waters prevail for a hundred and fifty days.
The Cup is poured out.
What remains is the vessel, and what it holds.
